The Wuji Hand is a next-generation robotic hand that takes a different approach than designs like Tesla’s Optimus or Figure 02. Instead of relying on tendon systems with motors placed in the forearm, Wuji embeds tiny actuators directly inside each finger. This gives it smoother, more predictable control, cutting down on the lag and calibration issues that often show up when moving from lab simulations to the real world.

It’s also built for durability and industrial use, with a mechanical design that favors reliability over fragility. While Optimus and Figure’s hands lean heavily on biomimicry, Wuji prioritizes consistent, repeatable performance—making it stronger, simpler to maintain, and easier to integrate into different robotic platforms.

The XPENG IRON robot is one of the most talked-about humanoid robots in the current AI robotics race. Its human-like AI robot design and unusually natural movement have made people compare it with Tesla Optimus and Boston Dynamics Atlas.

The humanoid robot uses XPENG’s physical AI approach, and the company says IRON is being developed toward mass production. XPENG has also showcased IRON alongside its broader physical AI technology, including its VLA systems.

What makes the XPENG IRON robot especially interesting is the attempt to make robotic movement feel less mechanical and more natural. That puts it directly into the conversation around embodied AI, physical AI, and humanoid robotics.

And yes, the human-like AI robot comparison is fascinating, but there’s an important distinction: looking human does not automatically mean thinking or acting like a human.

The humanoid robot race is moving quickly, with Tesla Optimus, Boston Dynamics Atlas, Figure, Unitree, and XPENG all pushing different approaches. XPENG currently says IRON is targeting formal mass production by the end of 2026, with initial retail deployment planned for 2027.

snippet.description:
Memo is a wheeled home robot from Sunday Robotics, a Mountain View startup founded by Stanford PhDs Tony Zhao and Cheng Chi. Unveiled in November 2025, it’s built to handle real household chores like loading the dishwasher, clearing tables, folding laundry, and even making espresso.

Standing about 5'7" and weighing 170 lbs, Memo moves on a stable wheeled base and uses a telescoping spine to reach up to 6'10". Instead of human-like hands, it has dual grippers designed for strength and precision, wrapped in a soft silicone shell to stay safe around kids, pets, and furniture. It runs for about 4 hours per charge, can recharge to 80% in an hour, and travels at up to 1 m/s.

Memo is powered by the ACT-1 foundation model, trained not on lab robots but on 10 million episodes of humans doing chores, captured with low-cost Skill Capture Gloves in over 500 homes. As a result, it can complete long, multi-step tasks—like a 33-step table-to-dishwasher routine—and generalize to new kitchens without teleoperation. Sunday is launching a 2026 beta with “Founding Families,” pitching Memo as a customizable, safe, skill-learning home appliance for single-floor homes.

In 2011, researchers in Japan developed a robotic mouth designed not to simulate speech digitally, but to physically reproduce how humans generate sound. Instead of speakers and software, the device uses an air pump that functions like artificial lungs to push air through a synthetic larynx, where vibrating “vocal cords” create the initial sound. That airflow is then shaped by a silicone tongue, lips, and a controllable nasal cavity, allowing it to mimic the acoustic processes of human speech production. By analyzing the sounds it produced and adjusting its movements, the system could gradually improve its clarity, offering scientists a rare, mechanical model for studying human phonetics, resonance, and articulation in real time.

Watching humanoid robots from China 🇨🇳 and the U.S. 🇺🇸 perform perfect backflips is impressive 🤸‍♂️—but does it really mean they’re more advanced than Boston Dynamics’ Atlas? 🤖

The truth is, robot size and purpose matter. Atlas is much larger and heavier, designed for real industrial work 🏗️—lifting, carrying, balancing heavy loads, and surviving harsh environments. As robot mass increases, movements like backflips become exponentially more complex due to physics, torque, impact forces, and safety constraints ⚙️📐

Lighter humanoids like Unitree H1 and H2 can showcase flashy acrobatics more easily 🎥✨, but that doesn’t make them better suited for factories, warehouses, or real-world deployment. Identical movements on screen can hide completely different engineering challenges and goals.

Backflips may go viral 🚀, but durability, strength, and reliability are what truly define next-generation humanoid robots.

This "embarrassing" moment is actually a great look at the complex engineering hurdles robotics companies still face with real-world terrain.

Despite its small size, it uses laser vision to map rooms and can even handle delicate objects with its robotic hands. These robots are built to be affordable and durable, aiming to move out of the lab and into the real world to assist people in factories or homes. By blending heavy duty hardware with smart software, Unitree is turning science fiction into a regular part of our daily lives.

"Roadrunner” is a new bipedal wheeled robot prototype designed for multi-modal locomotion. It weighs around 15kg (33 lb.) and can seamlessly switch between its side-by-side and in-line wheel modes and stepping configurations depending on what is required for navigating its environment. The robot’s legs are entirely symmetric, allowing it to point its knees forward or backward, which can be used to avoid obstacles or manage specific movements.

A single control policy was trained to handle both side-by-side and in-line driving. Several behaviors, including standing up from various ground configurations and balancing on one wheel, were successfully deployed zero-shot on the hardware.

1X Technologies, an OpenAI-backed startup founded in Norway and now based in Palo Alto, has opened a 58,000 square foot factory in Hayward, California, with capacity to build 10,000 NEO humanoid robots annually and plans to scale to 100,000 units by 2027. 

The $20,000 home robot is designed for chores like folding laundry and tidying up, and the company hopes it will eventually assist with elder care.

Unlike most competitors, 1X manufactures motors, batteries, and electronics in-house, a vertical integration strategy aimed at faster iteration and insulation from geopolitical supply chain risks.

The humanoid market is currently dominated by Chinese firms, which accounted for the majority of the roughly 13,000 units shipped worldwide last year, making 1X's US manufacturing push a notable counterweight. 

However, the company is openly acknowledging current limits: humans still perform most factory assembly, and NEO relies on remote human teleoperators to complete complex household tasks, with that data used to train its AI toward eventual full autonomy.

Human vs Robot: Humans Barely Won 12,924 Packages vs the Robot's 12,732

Description

Figure Al just tested its humanoid robot F.03 against a human intern in a real warehouse package sorting challenge and the results were surprisingly close.

The human sorted 12,924 packages. The robot sorted 12,732 packages.

That's a difference of only 192 packages after hours of nonstop work. No remote control. No teleoperation. Just autonomous Al-powered robotics operating in a real warehouse environment.

This is one of the clearest signs yet that humanoid robots are rapidly approaching human-level physical labor performance in logistics and warehouse automation. The future of Al robotics, autonomous workers, and warehouse automation is arriving much faster than most people expected.

The competition pushes AI systems to their limits by testing real-time perception, locomotion, balance, and autonomous decision-making under extreme physical stress.

The championship features a **10-kilogram solid gold title belt** valued at approximately **$1.4 million**, making it one of the most unique prizes in robotics. Qualified teams can register and develop their own AI software to control the identical robots, turning the event into a battle of algorithms rather than hardware.

Could these robots eventually rival human fighters? While legendary boxers like Mike Tyson still dominate in speed, instinct, and fight IQ, these machines are rapidly improving with every match. Each fight generates valuable data that helps train the next generation of humanoid robots for manufacturing, logistics, emergency response, and industrial automation.

Welcome to the future—where AI isn't just playing games anymore... it's stepping into the ring.

snippet.description:
What looks like robot hazing is actually a vital step in modern AI and hardware validation. Researchers from Shanghai-based robotics startup RoboParty are subjecting the Unitree G1 humanoid robot to intense physical stress, including repeated shoves, kicks, drags, and knockdowns, to test and refine its automated recovery systems.

The demonstration showcases UFO (A General Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning Framework for Humanoid Control). Instead of manually coding step-by-step instructions for balance, engineers train a digital twin of the robot inside a physics simulation. Through unsupervised learning, the AI tests millions of movement variations through trial and error, earning mathematical rewards for maintaining stability and recovering from unexpected falls.

Once the control policy is proven in the virtual world, it is deployed directly to the physical Unitree G1. This real-world physical abuse acts like an automotive crash test, exposing hardware limits and ensuring the locomotion policy can withstand chaotic, unpredictable environments without failing. According to developers, this approach cuts training time from several days down to just a few hours while reducing computational power requirements.

snippet.description:
A Chinese humanoid robot has run 100 metres in 9.39 seconds in a preliminary heat at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, surpassing the men's world record time held by Jamaican sprinting great Usain Bolt.

Tiangong Ultra, developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, won its heat at the opening of the games' second edition. The robot overtook ⁠smartphone maker Honor's Lightning near the finish after falling behind early in the race. Lightning finished in 9.47 seconds, also faster than the 9.58-second record Bolt set at the 2009 World Athletics Championships in Berlin.

The results marked a remarkable improvement from last year's inaugural games, when Tiangong Ultra won the 100 metres in 21.50 seconds. Tiangong also won the world's first humanoid robot half-marathon, held in Beijing last year.

The 100 metres is among 51 events at the games, which include football, dancing and  contests to complete industrial tasks.

China is promoting humanoid robots as a strategic emerging industry, with policymakers and companies betting that advances in AI and hardware will accelerate their use in manufacturing, logistics and consumer applications.

Investor enthusiasm for the sector was underscored recently when shares in Unitree, China's best-known humanoid robot maker, jumped more than five fold in its Shanghai trading debut, giving the company a market value of about $50 billion.

This year's ⁠games have drawn 2,056 robots from 666 teams across 16 countries and six continents, up from 280 teams at the inaugural event.

Clive Myrie presents BBC News at Ten reporting by Laura Bicker in Beijing.

Humanoid robots aren’t “coming soon” anymore — they’re already here, already shipping, and already being deployed in the real world. In this video, we break down six of the most important humanoid robots right now, each representing a totally different bet on what the future of robotics will look like: the warm, human-temperature companion android that creeps people out (DroidUp Moya), the production-ready factory worker that’s no longer a demo (Boston Dynamics Atlas), the robot that democratized robotics for researchers with a shockingly low entry price (Unitree G1), the company proving you can run multiple humanoids live at scale (AgiBot + Faraday Future-branded units), the car-company-built humanoid designed for mass manufacturing (XPENG Iron), and the fastest humanoid on Earth with verified records and real industrial capability (Robotera L7). We’ll cover the specs that actually matter (degrees of freedom, torque, payload, thermal design, sensors, compute TOPS, battery strategy), what these robots can do today (factory sequencing, package handling, inspection, research, demos that stress-test stability), and what the real “arms race” is shifting toward: shipping volume + reliability + developer ecosystems — not just flashy flips. If you want the most up-to-date, no-vaporware breakdown of AI robotics, humanoid robots 2026, and why this industry is compounding faster than anyone expected, this video is your roadmap.

Just months after its debut, Atlas is proving why it is the world’s most capable and dynamic humanoid robot, ready for real work. Lifting a mini-fridge is a feat of strength, but the true breakthrough is in the underlying reinforcement learning and controls systems. The robot is learning to navigate real world adaptability: handling heavy objects by bracing and accounting for the mass and inertia; using whole-body control, not just hands to maneuver; and demonstrating superhuman range of motion and balance. This marks a critical shift in robotics where humanoids move beyond the lab and into dynamic industrial settings.

Alberto Rodriguez, Director of Robot Behavior for Atlas, Shane Rozen-Levy, Research Engineer, and Vinay Kamidi, Research Engineer share more about training Atlas and developing robust, dynamic behaviors on our blog: https://bostondynamics.com/blog/training-a-humanoid-robot-for-hard-work/

Special thanks to Healthpeak for Atlas's outdoor walkabout!

What happens when work becomes optional?

For centuries, work has shaped our lives. It determines our routines, our status, our purpose, and often our identity. But what happens when artificial intelligence, robotics, and automation become so advanced that most jobs simply disappear?

This documentary explores a possible future in the year 2031 — a world where machines perform nearly every task once done by humans. Factories run themselves. Offices stand empty. Transportation, logistics, customer service, and even creative professions are increasingly automated.

At first glance, it sounds like a dream.

No alarms. No commutes. No deadlines.

But beneath the surface lies a far more complicated question:

If nobody needs to work... what gives life meaning?

Could universal basic income create a new golden age of freedom? Or would millions struggle with boredom, loss of purpose, and social isolation? Would humanity thrive, or would it face an existential crisis unlike anything in history?

Through realistic future scenarios, emerging technologies, economic trends, and psychological insights, this documentary explores one of the most important questions of the 21st century.

The future may arrive sooner than we think.

Stay curious! 🔍👇

snippet.description:
Robots used to struggle to walk, now they’re patrolling the streets. 

AI is what makes the headlines when it comes to job replacement but the industry quietly doing actual replacement is robotics. And thanks to the investment craze around AI, robotics has also received a financial boost. 

Here's a point I did not get into in the video. Notice how automation gets sold depending on whose job is on the line. When it comes for white-collar workers, the pitch is that it will handle the boring work. When it comes for blue-collar workers, the pitch is that it will handle the dangerous work. Either way, the framing is the same: it's here to help us, to take the parts of our job we didn't want anyway.

But that's the story they tell us, the public, who they need on board for our own replacements. The story they tell the corporations who they are actually selling to is much simpler: it cuts costs. The only problem is, we are the costs.

Human-AI relationships are no longer just science fiction. OpenAI’s launch of ChatGPT in 2022 ushered in a new era of artificial intelligence chatbots from companies like Nomi, Character AI and Replika, and tech titans like Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk are touting chatbots on their platforms. The AI companions have proven to be smart, quick-witted, argumentative, helpful and sometimes aggressively romantic. While some people are falling in love with the AI companions, others are building deep friendships. The speedy development of AI chatbots presents a mountain of ethical and safety concerns that experts say will only intensify once AI begins to train itself. The societal debate surrounding AI companions isn’t just about their effects on humans. Increasingly it’s about whether the companions can have human-like experiences. In this documentary, CNBC’s Salvador Rodriguez traveled across the U.S. to interview people who’ve formed emotional relationships with AI and met the founders of chatbot companies to explore the good, the bad and the unknown, and to find out how AI is changing relationships as we know them.

In this video, we explore the most high-tech things in the fastest growing tech-hub city in the world -Shenzhen!
 
Watch us try out tea deliveries via the sky, ghosts driving us in cars on highways, palm payments,  Xiaomi cars in their automotive flagship store, to robots serving us food. We even visit the high-tech fair to show you the kind of robots not yet available to buy in the market!

We stayed at Mandarin Oriental Shenzhen in the prime CBD area, so if you are interested in that it's in this video too! This was gifted via my Instagram. Nothing else in this video was sponsored or gifted, we paid for it all ourselves.

If you've visited before but over a year ago, this city has had THE most dramatic glow up in human history, so you will still find things you haven't seen before!

CHOOSE YOUR ROBOT CHAPTER:
00:00 Intro
01:14 Palm payments
01:40 Drone delivery
03:44 China’s Audi cars
04:38 Mandarin Oriental SZ room tour
05:21 Driverless taxi
08:02 Xiaomi cars (& Xiaomi 17 pro)
10:44 Robot served dinner
11:34 SZ Light show from MO Bar
13:08 Robot coffee
13:41 UFO Metro station
14:11 The Bay by Chef Fei
15:51 Fighting and dancing robots (27th Hi-Tech Fair)
18:20 Robot dolls
21:58 Cyberpunk viral street


Answering common questions here:

PALM PAYMENTS
You register your palm's patterns onto apps like Alipay or WeChat, like you register your Face ID onto your phone, and then you can use palm payments where available. It is not a chip in my hand. And it is not the ONLY method to pay, it's just the newest option to pay. They still take cash if that's your preferred method of payment.

THE LIGHT SHOW
Is at the Futian Civic Center runs primarily on Fridays and Saturdays only, plus Chinese public holidays, with three shows per night (7pm, 8pm, and 9pm in Winter; 7:30pm, 8:30pm, 9:30pm in Summer/Autumn)

DRONE DELIVERY
We saw reviews about it taking up to an hour to deliver, but it was only 10-15 mins for us, it could be down to the tea shop not being busy, or this specific drone location not being busy.
Apparently, drone delivery could lead to a ~80-95% reduction in single-use packaging waste and a ~50-85% reduction in last-mile carbon emissions per delivery for eligible packages compared to traditional home food and drink delivery.


If you have any questions, leave me a comment and I'll try get back to you!


Direct link for our hotel:
https://www.trip.com/t/cr14ybYCZS2

Follow me on Instagram:
http://instagram.com/heideexyz

Thanks for watching. Please subscribe and check out my other videos to support my channel and continue seeing videos from me!


Filmed in November, 2025

Brett Adcock is a technology entrepreneur focused on building companies in robotics, artificial intelligence, and aerospace. Born and raised on a third-generation farm in central Illinois, he developed an early fascination with technology and building systems from the ground up. After attending the University of Florida, he set out to tackle ambitious, capital-intensive industries with the goal of reshaping transportation, labor, and human-machine collaboration.

At 26, Adcock founded Vettery, an AI-powered talent marketplace that matched thousands of companies with highly qualified candidates. The company scaled rapidly and was acquired in 2018 for $110 million by The Adecco Group, the world’s largest recruiting firm.

In 2018, he founded Archer Aviation to develop electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft aimed at transforming urban air mobility. During his time leading the company, Adcock helped architect, engineer, and flight-test five generations of aircraft, vertically integrating key technologies including flight software, electric motors, actuation systems, and battery systems. Archer secured a $1.5 billion partnership with United Airlines and positioned itself at the forefront of next-generation aviation.

In 2022, Adcock founded Figure, where he serves as Founder & CEO. Figure is building general-purpose humanoid robots designed to address global labor shortages and work alongside humans in manufacturing, logistics, warehousing, retail, and the home. Backed by leading investors including Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital, the company has raised billions in venture capital and is focused on deploying embodied AI systems at scale.

He is also the founder of Cover (2023–present), an AI security company developing non-intrusive scanners in partnership with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The technology is designed to passively detect concealed weapons in crowded environments, with the goal of improving public safety without invasive screening.

Brett Adcock is a technology entrepreneur focused on building companies in robotics, artificial intelligence, and aerospace. Born and raised on a third-generation farm in central Illinois, he developed an early fascination with technology and building systems from the ground up. After attending the University of Florida, he set out to tackle ambitious, capital-intensive industries with the goal of reshaping transportation, labor, and human-machine collaboration.

At 26, Adcock founded Vettery, an AI-powered talent marketplace that matched thousands of companies with highly qualified candidates. The company scaled rapidly and was acquired in 2018 for $110 million by The Adecco Group, the world’s largest recruiting firm.

In 2018, he founded Archer Aviation to develop electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft aimed at transforming urban air mobility. During his time leading the company, Adcock helped architect, engineer, and flight-test five generations of aircraft, vertically integrating key technologies including flight software, electric motors, actuation systems, and battery systems. Archer secured a $1.5 billion partnership with United Airlines and positioned itself at the forefront of next-generation aviation.

In 2022, Adcock founded Figure, where he serves as Founder & CEO. Figure is building general-purpose humanoid robots designed to address global labor shortages and work alongside humans in manufacturing, logistics, warehousing, retail, and the home. Backed by leading investors including Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital, the company has raised billions in venture capital and is focused on deploying embodied AI systems at scale.

He is also the founder of Cover (2023–present), an AI security company developing non-intrusive scanners in partnership with NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. As a hidden tech empire prepares an army of cybernetic predators, the survivors must escape underground laboratories, stop a catastrophic core overload, and face a growing force of robot cats, mechanical wolves, combat birds, armored rhinos, and other deadly mecha beasts.

The battle eventually leads to a frozen military base, where the final Living Key could either end the machine war—or give artificial intelligence complete control.

Watch to the end for the final Arctic confrontation and the choice that determines whether these mechanical animals remain weapons or become something more.

Emad Mostaque founded Stability AI, built Stable Diffusion, and helped kick off the open-source generative AI explosion - before stepping down to build a new blueprint for human freedom as founder and CEO of Intelligent Internet. A former hedge fund manager turned tech pioneer, he argues that we have reached the end of our "economic life expectancy," and that within two years, virtually any job that can be done remotely will be done cheaper, faster, and better by artificial intelligence.  

Emad and I discuss why 50% of work tasks are about to collapse like a sand pile, the arrival of $1.50-an-hour humanoid robots that fit directly into human-shaped holes, and why the state will inevitably try to license AI and use brain-scanning technology to prevent you from lying.
